extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of mathematics, logic, and foundations; mathematicians interested in Wittgenstein's views
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Wittgenstein's intermediate-period standards for what counts as a mathematical proposition, acceptable methods (e.g., induction, decision procedures), genuine irrational numbers, and the status of set theory and infinite quantification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful mathematical proposition iff decided or decidable in a calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: An expression is a meaningful (genuine) proposition of a mathematical calculus iff we know of a proof, a refutation, or an applicable decision procedure (PR §151; PG 452; PG 366; AWL 199–200).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein defines both a mathematical calculus and a mathematical proposition in epistemic terms: a calculus is stipulated by known rules and decision procedures, and an expression counts as a mathematical proposition only if it is already decided or known to be decidable by an applicable procedure. If no such procedure is known, the expression is not a mathematical proposition (it is 'senseless').

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of unrestricted quantification (infinite domains are meaningless)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions that quantify over an infinite domain (e.g., '∀n …' or '∃n …') are never meaningful mathematical propositions; such quantified 'propositions' are senseless (PR §§127, 150, 168).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'There exists an odd perfect number' taken as an infinite disjunction is misleading; an existential or universal quantifier over an infinite domain does not yield a genuine proposition because the Law of Excluded Middle does not apply and there is no algorithmic way to 'check' the infinite series. Even God cannot 'survey' an infinite series according to Wittgenstein's point about tasks that have no end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic decidability as the test for mathematical sense
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical expression has sense only if we know of an applicable (algorithmic) decision procedure that will prove or refute it (PG 400; PG 468).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein emphasizes that 'In mathematics everything is algorithm and nothing is meaning' and that 'we can assert anything which can be checked in practice'—so explanations of mathematicality must appeal to concrete methods of decision (algorithms). Where such a method is known, the proposition can be handled as a mathematical proposition; where it is not, the expression lacks mathematical sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish four categories of symbolic concatenations
rubrics_metrics.description: Wittgenstein distinguishes: (1) proved mathematical propositions in a calculus; (2) refuted propositions in a calculus; (3) propositions for which we know an applicable and effective decision procedure; (4) concatenations that are not part of any calculus and thus are non-propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxonomy demarcates genuine mathematical expressions from non-propositions. Wittgenstein's fourth category (non-propositions) is crucially different from Brouwer's corresponding list and underpins his rejection of meaningful undecidable propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undecidable expressions are not mathematical propositions (contradiction-in-terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: There cannot be 'undecidable propositions' in mathematics; if an expression is not decidable in some actual calculus, it is simply not a mathematical proposition (PR §173).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein argues that 'undecidability' presupposes a bridge to be made with symbols that cannot be represented by symbolic transformations; such a 'thought' cannot be thought. Hence, alleged undecidable mathematical propositions lack sense and the logical laws (including LEM) do not apply to them as mathematical propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: A calculus is defined epistemically (by stipulations, known rules, and decision procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical calculus consists of stipulations, known rules of operation, and known (applicable) decision procedures (PR §202; PG 369).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Wittgenstein defines calculi in terms of what is known how to operate, membership of a proposition in mathematics is tied to epistemic access to rules/procedures. This yields the criterion that only expressions that can be situated inside such a calculus count as mathematical propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction is not itself a proposition; proofs by induction establish a proxy, not ∀nφ(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: An induction is 'the expression for arithmetical generality' but it 'isn't itself a proposition' (PR §129); an inductive proof yields a proxy statement φ(m) standing for particular instances rather than the universal ∀nφ(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein's reconstruction of induction: Inductive base φ(1) and step φ(n)→φ(n+1) allow us to 'perceive' how to construct a direct proof of any particular φ(m). The customary universal conclusion is a pseudo-proposition serving as a shorthand or proxy for the induction and does not assert an extensional infinite generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs (and new proofs) give propositions their determinate sense and place
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof locates a proposition 'in the whole system of calculations' and a new proof 'gives the proposition a place in a new system'—the sense of a proposition is altered or fixed by its proof (RFM VI, §11; §13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On Wittgenstein's view, the sense of a mathematical expression is not fully determinate antecedently; constructing a proof can create a new calculus (or machine-part) in which the expression acquires determinate sense. Thus mathematical meaning is dynamic and proof-relative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical problems/questions only where there is a method of solution
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Only where there's a method of solution is there a [mathematical] problem' (PR §§149, 152).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We may only legitimately pose mathematical questions or conjectures where the answer is of the form 'I must work it out'; in other cases (no method known) the expression is not a genuine mathematical question/proposition. This relates to the insistence on algorithmic decidability as criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: No syntax–semantics split: mathematics is exclusively syntax (rules/algorithms)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Wittgenstein there is no real distinction between syntax and semantics in mathematics: everything is syntax; mathematical expressions are rules or operations rather than carriers of independent semantic content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This underlies his demarcation between genuine propositions (as calculi-embedded rules) and pseudo-propositions; it motivates his skepticism about talking of mathematical 'truth' independent of calculational procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real (genuine) irrational numbers must be comparable with any rational and 'measure in and of itself'
rubrics_metrics.description: A real number must be 'comparable with any rational number taken at random' (i.e., it can be established whether it is greater than, less than, or equal to a rational number) and 'a number must measure in and of itself'—if a 'number' leaves it to rationals, 'we have no need of it' (PR §191).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein uses these criteria to exclude many constructed or 'pseudo-' irrationals: genuine irrationals are rule-governed numerals that can be used for measurement; those that fail comparability or self-measurement are not genuine real numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject pseudo-irrationals and 'lawless' irrationals that are notation-dependent or non-rule-governed
rubrics_metrics.description: Recursive/computable reals that are dependent on incidental notation (e.g., replacing digits in sqrt(2) to make a new 'number') or 'lawless' (free-choice sequences) are not genuine irrationals (PR §§180–186, 191; PG 475–476).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: π' defined by altering decimal digits of π (5→3 or 777→000) is 'homeless' and notation-dependent; lawless irrationals are not rule-governed and so fail to be comparable or useful for measurement. Wittgenstein argues such creations are unnecessary and misleading for a theory of the continuum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics should not be extended by unnecessary constructions (anti-foundationalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wittgenstein opposes extending arithmetic/real analysis via foundationalist inventions (pseudo-irrationals, lawless sequences) created to 'fill gaps' imagined by set theory; such extensions are unnecessary and engender confusions (PG 471; PR §§171, 173).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He contends that set-theoretic completions (adding pseudo- or lawless irrationals) do not add needed content to calculus or analysis; rather, they misrepresent the number line and foster conceptual mistakes born of mistaken pictures of continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of set theory: law vs enumeration distinction and 'fictitious symbolism'
rubrics_metrics.description: Set theory's practice of treating laws (rules) and enumerations (lists) as the same kind of thing is a fundamental mistake; this leads to a 'fictitious symbolism' for the infinite and makes set theory 'nonsense' or 'wrong' (PR §§170–174; PG 468–469).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein argues you cannot substitute intension (a description) for extension (an actual enumeration), and attempting to 'describe' the infinite class (e.g., Dedekind's definition) is laughable or nonsensical because one cannot coordinate or attempt the relevant infinite procedure. Thus transfinite set theory rests on misleading idioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical expressions must be usable in a calculational practice (application criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical expressions/proposals are legitimate only insofar as they can be situated in a calculus and used in calculational practice; purely formal sign-games without applicability are to be demarcated from mathematical calculi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Late-middle Wittgenstein's tension between formalism and rejection of set theory leads to an extra-mathematical application criterion: if a formalism cannot be applied in calculational practice (i.e., no rules/decision procedures), it should not be treated as genuine mathematics.
